title: TOFD Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: Free 30-Question Test
metaDescription: 30 original TOFD Level II practice questions with answers: diffraction, PCS set-up, calibration, B-scan reading, depth and height sizing, dead zones.
h1: Time-of-Flight Diffraction (TOFD) Level II Practice Questions
intro: These 30 multiple-choice questions are original study questions written by Atlantis NDT for ultrasonic technicians working toward Level II in time-of-flight diffraction. They are not ASNT exam questions. They follow the Level II job: choose probes and set the probe center separation, calibrate on the lateral wave and back wall, acquire encoded data, interpret the B-scan, size flaws from arrival times and report against a procedure.

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition), the employer certifies Level II technicians after general, specific and practical examinations defined in its written practice, which sets the TOFD training and experience it requires. ASNT's central ASNT NDT Level II examinations include UT but do not list TOFD as a separate technique, so the TOFD examinations come from the employer's written practice. A good grounding in conventional UT is assumed.

Atlantis NDT runs NDT training year-round, with theory online and hands-on practice on its Practical NDT simulator or in person at the client's own facility. Simulator practice supports training; it does not replace the practical examination or the experience hours the employer's written practice requires.
howToUse: Answer each question before opening the explanation.
For the sizing questions, draw the two probes, the tip and the two half-paths; the depth falls out of a right-angled triangle.
Keep units consistent: velocity in mm/µs (5.9 for steel longitudinal) makes the arithmetic quick.
Note the topics where you miss questions, study them against your employer's TOFD procedure, then re-test.

questions.q: Which signal from a flaw does TOFD mainly rely on for detection and sizing?
options: Specular reflection from the flaw face
Diffracted signals from the flaw tips
Loss of through-transmitted amplitude only
Surface waves generated at the flaw
questions.explanation: When sound strikes the tip of a crack-like flaw, diffracted energy spreads over a wide range of angles. TOFD records these weak tip signals and uses their arrival times, rather than echo amplitude, to locate and size the flaw.

questions.q: Why is TOFD height sizing less dependent on flaw orientation than amplitude-based sizing?
options: Because TOFD uses shear waves, which are not affected by orientation
Because the instrument automatically corrects amplitude for orientation
Because diffraction is weakly directional and sizing uses arrival times
Because TOFD can only detect flaws perpendicular to the surface
questions.explanation: Diffraction from a tip is weak but not strongly directional, and the depth of each tip is calculated from its arrival time. The echo amplitude, which depends heavily on orientation, is not used for sizing.

questions.q: In a TOFD A-scan with longitudinal-wave probes, which signal normally arrives first?
options: The lateral wave, just below the surface between the probes
The back-wall echo, reflected from the far surface of the plate
The upper-tip signal from a flaw at mid-wall, if one is present
The mode-converted shear back-wall signal
questions.explanation: The lateral wave takes the shortest path, directly between the probes just beneath the surface, so it arrives first. Tip signals from flaws follow, then the back-wall echo, then the slower mode-converted signals.

questions.q: How do the diffracted signals from the upper and lower tips of an embedded crack normally compare in phase?
options: In phase with each other, since both come from the same flaw
Opposite in phase, the upper tip matching the back wall
Only the upper tip gives a signal; the lower tip is shadowed
Their phase depends only on the probe frequency and the PCS
questions.explanation: The upper and lower tip signals are 180° apart in phase. The lateral wave and back-wall echo are also opposite in phase, and the upper tip normally matches the back wall while the lower tip matches the lateral wave, which helps identify each tip.

questions.q: Which signals in a TOFD A-scan arrive after the longitudinal back-wall echo?
options: The lateral wave, which travels the longest path
Upper-tip signals from flaws lying just below the scanning surface
The initial transmitter pulse, delayed by the wedges
Mode-converted shear-wave signals, such as the shear back wall
questions.explanation: Mode conversion at flaws and at the back wall produces shear-wave components that travel more slowly than longitudinal waves, so they arrive after the longitudinal back wall. The region of interest therefore arrives before the mode-converted signals.

questions.q: What probe arrangement is normally used for TOFD weld examination?
options: A single shear-wave probe in pulse-echo mode, scanned from both sides of the weld
A 0° dual-element probe scanned along the weld cap
A longitudinal-wave transmitter and receiver facing each other across the weld
Two surface-wave probes placed side by side on one side of the weld
questions.explanation: TOFD is a pitch-catch technique: one probe transmits, the other receives the lateral wave, tip diffractions and back wall. The pair straddles the weld so the beams cover the weld volume.

questions.q: Why are longitudinal waves used rather than shear waves for TOFD?
options: They arrive first, ahead of all slower mode-converted signals
Shear waves cannot be diffracted by the tip of a crack
Longitudinal waves do not spread, so the beam stays narrow
Shear waves are absorbed completely in carbon steel welds
questions.explanation: Longitudinal waves are the fastest mode, so the lateral wave, tip signals and back wall all arrive before any mode-converted signals and the time window is simple to interpret. Shear waves do diffract at crack tips and do travel through carbon steel welds, and longitudinal beams spread like any other; shear waves are simply slower.

questions.q: Why are highly damped, broadband probes used for TOFD?
options: To increase the refracted angle of the beam in the part
To give short pulses for good depth resolution and smaller dead zones
To make the lateral wave disappear from the display
To allow the probes to work without couplant on smooth, clean plate
questions.explanation: Short pulses allow closely spaced signals, such as two tips of a small flaw or a tip just below the lateral wave, to be separated in time. Long ringing pulses enlarge the dead zones and blur the tip signals.

questions.q: For a 30 mm thick plate with 60° probes, what probe center separation (PCS) places the beam intersection at two-thirds of the thickness?
questions.explanation: PCS = 2 × (2/3 × T) × tan θ = 2 × 20 × tan 60° = 40 × 1.732 ≈ 69.3 mm. Setting the intersection at the full thickness would give 103.9 mm, and 34.6 mm is only half the required separation.
questions.ref: TOFD set-up geometry (common practice: intersection at about 2/3 T)

questions.q: Why are thick welds often examined with more than one TOFD probe pair or scan, each set up for a different depth zone?
options: Because one pair cannot cover the whole thickness with enough resolution
Because TOFD can only detect flaws exactly at the beam intersection point
Because the encoder can only record a limited depth range
Because the back-wall echo must be excluded from every scan
questions.explanation: Beam spread, attenuation and resolution all vary with depth, so thick sections are divided into zones, each with its own probe angle, frequency and PCS. A single pair still covers more than just the intersection point, but not the full thickness well.

questions.q: Why is TOFD gain commonly set so that low-level grain noise is just visible across the display?
options: To make the back-wall echo saturate so it is easy to see
Because diffracted tip signals are weak and need high sensitivity
To remove the lateral wave from the top of the display
Because the grain noise is needed to calibrate the encoder distance
questions.explanation: Tip diffractions are much weaker than reflections from flaw faces. Setting gain so that material noise is just visible shows the system is sensitive enough to record weak tip signals; the procedure defines the exact sensitivity setting.

questions.q: Where should the TOFD acquisition time window normally start and end?
options: Start at the back-wall echo and end at the shear back wall
Start just after the lateral wave and end just before the back-wall echo
Start before the lateral wave and end after the back-wall echo
Start at the initial pulse and end at the lateral wave
questions.explanation: The window must contain every signal that can come from the examined volume, from the lateral wave (scanning surface) to the back wall. Including the mode-converted region helps confirm indications near the back wall. The procedure or standard sets the exact margins.

questions.q: Why must the digitization (sampling) rate be several times higher than the probe's nominal frequency?
options: To increase the penetration of the probe into the weld
To reduce the size of each data file
To capture the waveform shape and phase faithfully for sizing
Because the encoder needs a high sampling rate to count distance
questions.explanation: TOFD relies on accurate arrival times and on phase to identify tips. Under-sampling distorts the waveform and introduces timing errors. Higher sampling increases file size rather than reducing it.

questions.q: Why is the TOFD set-up checked on a reference block containing reflectors such as notches or side-drilled holes at known depths before scanning?
options: To confirm coverage, sensitivity and depth calibration
To measure the hardness of the weld and heat-affected zone
To determine the client's acceptance criteria for the weld
To set the scanner speed only
questions.explanation: Known reflectors at the top, middle and bottom of the zone show that the beams reach them, that their signals are visible at the chosen gain and that the calculated depths are right. Acceptance criteria come from the code or specification.

questions.q: On the component, the lateral wave and back-wall arrival times are measured with a known plate thickness and PCS. What can these two signals be used to calibrate?
options: The probe frequency and the pulse bandwidth
The weld acceptance level for the scan
The encoder resolution and scan increment
The probe delay and the depth scale
questions.explanation: The lateral wave corresponds to zero depth and the back wall to the known thickness. With the PCS known, these two references fix the time zero (probe delay) and the velocity used to convert arrival times into depths.

questions.q: How does an embedded planar flaw typically appear in a TOFD B-scan (D-scan) image?
options: As a break in the lateral wave, with no signal between it and the back wall
As a break in the back-wall echo, with no signal between it and the lateral wave
As a single short hyperbolic arc with no measurable depth extent
As two opposite-phase tip signals, with the lateral wave and back wall undisturbed
questions.explanation: An embedded flaw with measurable height has two tips, each producing its own diffraction signal, and it does not interrupt the lateral wave or the back wall. A single short arc is typical of a point reflector.

questions.q: How does a flaw breaking the scanning surface typically appear in TOFD?
options: As a break in the lateral wave plus a lower-tip signal
As two separate tip signals below an undisturbed lateral wave
As a break in the back-wall echo, with the lateral wave intact
As a signal arriving after the mode-converted shear back wall
questions.explanation: A flaw open to the scanning surface interrupts the lateral wave path; its only separate tip is the lower one. Its upper end is at the surface, inside the lateral wave.

questions.q: How does a crack open to the back wall (inside surface) typically appear in TOFD?
options: As a lower-tip signal only, with an undisturbed back wall
As an upper-tip signal plus a break in the back-wall echo
As an interruption of the lateral wave only
No signal appears, since TOFD cannot detect such flaws
questions.explanation: The crack's lower end is at the back wall, so instead of a lower-tip signal the back-wall echo is disturbed or shadowed beneath the flaw. The upper tip gives a diffraction signal above it.

questions.q: How does a point reflector, such as an isolated pore, typically appear in a non-parallel TOFD scan?
options: As a long flat line parallel to the lateral wave
As a break in the back-wall echo
As a short hyperbolic arc with little depth extent
As a disturbance of the lateral wave
questions.explanation: As the probes approach and pass a point reflector, the arrival time first decreases and then increases, producing a characteristic hyperbolic arc. It has no measurable height, unlike a planar flaw with separate upper and lower tips.

questions.q: Why is the phase of TOFD signals useful during interpretation?
options: It shows the probe frequency actually achieved
It indicates the flaw's chemical composition, such as slag or oxide
It replaces the need for an encoder on short scans
It shows whether a signal is an upper or a lower tip
questions.explanation: Because upper and lower tips give opposite phases, the analyst can tell whether a single signal is an upper tip (suggesting a back-wall-breaking flaw) or a lower tip (suggesting a scanning-surface-breaking flaw), and can pair the tips of an embedded flaw.

questions.q: Over a short section of the scan, the lateral wave and the back-wall echo both disappear. What is the most likely cause?
options: A large embedded crack between the two probes
Loss of coupling, so that section must be rescanned
A lamination at mid-thickness under both probes
Normal behavior; these signals often fade on thick plate
questions.explanation: An embedded flaw does not remove the lateral wave, and a mid-wall lamination would block the back wall but not the lateral wave. Losing both together points to coupling, and the data in that section cannot be evaluated.

questions.q: A TOFD set-up uses a PCS of 80 mm on steel (longitudinal velocity 5,900 m/s). After removing the probe delay, a tip signal arrives at 16.95 µs. What is the depth of the tip, assuming it lies midway between the probes?
questions.explanation: Total path = 5.9 mm/µs × 16.95 µs ≈ 100 mm, so each half-path is 50 mm. With half the PCS S = 40 mm, depth d = √(50² − 40²) = √900 = 30.0 mm. 50 mm is the half-path, not the depth.

questions.q: In the same set-up (PCS 80 mm, 5,900 m/s), the upper tip of a flaw is at 30.0 mm depth and the lower-tip signal arrives at 19.66 µs. What is the flaw height?
options: 2.7 mm
8.0 mm
questions.explanation: Total path = 5.9 × 19.66 ≈ 116 mm, half-path 58 mm. Lower-tip depth = √(58² − 40²) = √1,764 = 42.0 mm. Height = 42.0 − 30.0 = 12.0 mm. Height is a difference in depth, not the difference in path or time.

questions.q: How is flaw length normally measured in a non-parallel TOFD scan?
options: From the time difference between the upper and lower tip signals
From the peak amplitude of the A-scan at the flaw center
From the duration of the lateral wave signal in the A-scan
Along the scan axis, with hyperbolic cursors fitted to the ends
questions.explanation: Length lies along the encoded scan axis. Because beam spread makes the ends trail off as arcs, hyperbolic cursors are fitted to the ends rather than reading where the signal visibly fades. The tip time difference gives height, not length.

questions.q: In a non-parallel TOFD scan, the depth calculation assumes the flaw lies midway between the probes. What is the effect if the flaw is actually off-center?
options: The depth is overestimated, because an off-center tip has a longer path
There is no effect, because TOFD depth is independent of lateral position
The flaw cannot be detected at all by the receiver
The calculated height doubles but depth is unchanged
questions.explanation: For a given depth, the sound path is shortest at the midpoint between the probes. An off-center tip has a longer path, so the midpoint assumption gives a depth greater than the true depth. A parallel scan or offset scans can be used to locate the flaw laterally.

questions.q: Why are flaws very close to the scanning surface difficult to detect and size with TOFD?
options: Their signals arrive after the back wall and are outside the window
Diffraction does not occur at tips close to the surface
Their tip signals arrive within the lateral wave and are masked
The encoder cannot record positions for near-surface signals
questions.explanation: The lateral wave has a finite duration, and signals from tips just below the surface arrive within it. Higher frequency, shorter pulses or a smaller PCS shrink this dead zone, and supplementary techniques such as pulse-echo UT or PAUT are commonly used to cover it.

questions.q: What limits TOFD detection of small flaws very close to the back wall?
options: Their tip signals are masked by the back-wall echo
The lateral wave interferes with them
Mode-converted signals arrive before them and hide them
Longitudinal waves cannot reach the back wall of thick plate
questions.explanation: A tip signal that arrives within the duration of the back-wall echo cannot be separated from it, which creates a back-wall dead zone. The mode-converted signals arrive after, not before, the longitudinal back wall.

questions.q: Which pair of standards specifically addresses TOFD examination of welds?
options: ASTM E2700 and ISO 13588
ASTM E2373 and ISO 10863
ASTM E309 and ASTM E426
ASTM E1444 and ISO 9934
questions.explanation: ASTM E2373 and ISO 10863 cover TOFD. ASTM E2700 and ISO 13588 cover phased array UT of welds, ASTM E309 and E426 cover eddy current examination of tubular products, and ASTM E1444 and the ISO 9934 series cover magnetic particle testing.

questions.q: Which joint condition makes a standard TOFD scan difficult or impossible?
options: A flat butt weld with clear access on both sides on the same surface
A weld with the cap ground flush to the plate surface
A nozzle or tee joint without access to both sides on one surface
A plate thicker than the probe's near-field length
questions.explanation: Standard TOFD needs the transmitter and receiver on opposite sides of the weld on the same surface. Where geometry prevents that, other techniques or special configurations are needed. A flush cap actually helps scanning.

questions.q: Which information should a TOFD report contain so the examination can be reproduced?
options: The list of rejected indications with their positions
The operator's name, the date and the client's order number
Probes, PCS, time window, sensitivity, reference block, scan plan and data file
The color palette and print settings used for the images
questions.explanation: Another qualified technician must be able to rebuild the set-up and coverage from the report, and the data file must be traceable to it. Indications, the operator and the date are recorded too, but alone they do not allow the examination to be repeated.
questions.ref: General NDT reporting practice; ASTM E2373
